She is under the cart with a strap in her teeth, in the rain, at four in the morning, and does not come out when she hears you.

"If you're here about the dead man," she says around the strap, "I was asleep, I'm glad, and I'd have done it cheaper."

"Glad." The strap comes out of her teeth. "He took forty pounds of undeclared tin off me at the Kelder toll on Tuesday and wrote it in his little book, and that tin was three months of the year. So yes. Glad. Write that down."

She comes out. Slowly, and streaming, and looking at you with a kind of grudging recalculation.

"Forty pounds of tin," she says. "Undeclared, off the back of this cart, at the Kelder toll on Tuesday. In his book. Three months of my year in his book." She wipes her face. "That's my motive. You'd have found it. Now ask me the other thing."

She does not come out. The strap goes back between her teeth.

"Tin," she says. "Forty pound of it, off this cart, Tuesday, and in his book. There's your reason and you can have it standing in the rain like everyone else."
Rain runs off the cart's edge between you in a line.
